title.text:
Open weights, file formats,
size and running cost

objects.text: What does it mean to own, host or rent a model?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 7 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 7. Last time you met the families of foundation models. Today we open the file. A model you can download is a very large file of numbers, and its size, its licence and its format decide whether you rent it, host it or own it.

I will show real file sizes that I measured on this machine, and you will leave with a decision sheet.

And you can choose rent, host or own for one of your own tasks and say why. Nothing here needs coding. The multiplication is the hardest step.

title.text: Your two hours: numbers first, then the decision

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_08217901.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: You do the memory sum by hand and fill the decision sheet yourself.

slides.notes:
Today has three big parts. First, thirty-five minutes on the ideas: what open weights means, what a weights file is, how its size comes from a simple multiplication, and why containers and quantisation are different things. Then twenty-five minutes of demonstrations with real file sizes that I measured on this laptop.

After the break you work the memory sum on paper and fill a rent, host or own sheet for a task of your own.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is the difference between pretraining and post-training?
2.  What can a benchmark tell you about a model, and what can it not tell you?
3.  Name two things you can read on a model card.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 6. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is the difference between pretraining and post-training? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Pretraining reads a huge library of text to learn the patterns of language. Post-training then coaches the model to follow instructions and give helpful answers.

Question two. What can a benchmark tell you about a model, and what can it not tell you? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. It compares models on a standard set of questions, which helps a shortlist. It does not test your own documents or risks, so you test the finalists on your own examples.

Question three. Name two things you can read on a model card. Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. What the makers say the model is for, how it was built at a high level, how they tested it, its known limits and its licence.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A model whose trained numbers you may download and run, under a licence that can still limit use.
The numbers inside a model, set during training. Also called parameters.
Rounding each weight to fewer allowed values, so each one needs fewer bits and the file shrinks.
The file format that packs the numbers: Safetensors, GGUF or ONNX.
Running a model on a server you rent, so you choose where your data goes.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Open weights. A model whose trained numbers you may download and run, under a licence that can still limit use.

Weights. The numbers inside a model, set during training. Also called parameters.

Quantisation. Rounding each weight to fewer allowed values, so each one needs fewer bits and the file shrinks.

Container. The file format that packs the numbers: Safetensors, GGUF or ONNX.

Hosting. Running a model on a server you rent, so you choose where your data goes.

title.text:
Open weights means you can download
the numbers; open source asks for more

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_openness_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Open weights means you can download the numbers; open source asks for more

objects.text: The OSI definition of Open Source AI needs all four.

runs.text: The OSI is the Open Source Initiative. Its AI definition, version 1.0, dates from 2024.
Data information is a detailed description of the training data. The data itself need not be shared.

slides.notes:
Think of a cake. Open weights is the finished cake you may take home. Open source AI is the cake, the recipe and the shopping list, with a licence that lets you bake it for any purpose. The Open Source Initiative published its Open Source AI Definition, version 1.0, in 2024.

It asks for the weights, the complete code used to train and run the system, and enough information about the training data for a skilled person to build a similar system. And all of it under terms that let you use it for any purpose. Most downloadable models give you the first item only.

title.text:
A licence with conditions makes a model
open weights, however free the download

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_licence_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A licence with conditions makes a model open weights, however free the download

objects.text: Llama 3.2 licence, read on 6 November 2026. Check the version in force.

slides.notes:
Here is a real example. Meta lets you download its Llama weights for free. The Llama 3.2 licence still has conditions. A company with more than 700 million monthly users must ask Meta for a licence. You must show Built with Llama if you distribute it, follow Meta’s Acceptable Use Policy, and start the name of a model made with it with the word Llama.

The Open Source Initiative said in 2023 that the Llama licence is not open source because it limits some users and some uses, and its director repeated this in October 2024. So call such models open weights. This is not legal advice, so read the licence you will use.

title.text: Weights are a very large file of numbers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_weightsfile_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Weights are a very large file of numbers

objects.text: A model is a file of numbers. Each number is a weight.

runs.text: Weights are the parameters that training adjusted, as in Session 0.
This small model has 134,515,008 of them.

slides.notes:
Picture a mixing desk with 134 million sliders. Training set every slider. The model file is simply the list of where each slider sits. This grid is real. I read the first numbers from the first layer of a small open model called SmolLM2, published under the Apache 2.0 licence.

Each number is a weight, also called a parameter. This one has 134,515,008. The larger open models on the next slides have billions, hundreds of times more. The file holds no words and no documents. It holds numbers, and the program that runs it turns your question into numbers and back.

title.text:
File size is the number of weights
times the bytes each one takes

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_memorysum_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: File size is the number of weights times the bytes each one takes

objects.text: 134.5 million numbers times 4 bytes each is 538 MB.

runs.text: A byte is one unit of storage. Eight bits make one byte.
I measured the real file: 538,090,376 bytes.

slides.notes:
Now the arithmetic, and it is a shop sum. A stockroom holds 134.5 million items, and each item takes four shelf slots. How many slots?

Multiply. In a model the items are weights and a slot is a byte. In the common 32-bit form each weight takes four bytes. So 134.5 million times four is about 538 million bytes, 538 megabytes. I then wrote the real file and measured it: 538,090,376 bytes. The small extra is the file header. Remember the sentence: parameters times bytes per number equals size.

title.text:
The same sum shows why big
models need big machines

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_scale_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The same sum shows why big models need big machines

objects.text: Arithmetic only: numbers x 2 bytes (16-bit) or x half a byte (4-bit). Weights only.

slides.notes:
Apply the same multiplication to bigger models. One billion numbers at two bytes each is two gigabytes. Seven billion is fourteen. Seventy billion is one hundred and forty gigabytes, which no ordinary laptop holds. Halve the bytes and you halve the memory, and four bits is half a byte, so seventy billion shrinks to thirty-five gigabytes.

This is the arithmetic of the weights alone. A running model also needs working memory for your conversation, so real needs are higher. Do not trust any claim about running a model on a given machine until the sum has been done.

title.text:
Quantisation rounds each number
to one of fewer allowed values

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_levels_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Quantisation rounds each number to one of fewer allowed values

objects.text: Like quoting a price to the nearest UGX 1,000 instead of to the shilling.

runs.text: Fewer allowed values need fewer bits, so the file shrinks.
The rounding loses a little precision. That is the price of the smaller file.

slides.notes:
Think of a shop that rounds every price. Exact prices need many digits. Prices rounded to the nearest one thousand shillings need fewer, and the till tape is shorter, but each price is a little off. Quantisation does that to every weight. With 8 bits a weight can take one of 256 values.

With 4 bits it can take only 16. In the picture the number 0.37 is stored as 0.37 at 8 bits and as 0.33 at 4 bits. Across 134 million weights the small errors mostly cancel, but not always, and we measure that in a moment.

title.text:
Containers and quantisation
are two separate choices

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_container_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Containers and quantisation are two separate choices

objects.text: GGUF is a container. 4-bit is a compression level. A GGUF file can hold either.

slides.notes:
This is the point executives most often get wrong. In a court bundle, the binder is the container, and how sharp the photographs are is a separate choice. Safetensors is a container for the numbers, built to load safely. GGUF packs the numbers with settings in one file, and local tools such as llama.cpp read it.

ONNX packs the numbers with the calculation, so a model can move between tools. Quantisation is the other row, how many bits each number gets. A vendor who says we ship GGUF has told you the box and nothing about the size.

title.text:
Same model, three containers:
the size follows the bits

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_sizegrid_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Same model, three containers: the size follows the bits

objects.text: At 16-bit all three are about 270 MB. The 4-bit files differ: ask which method.

slides.notes:
Here is the proof, read from the real file lists on Hugging Face today. This is the same small model in three containers. At 16-bit it is about 270 megabytes in all three. At 8-bit it is between 135 and 145. The container did not change the size, the bits did.

At 4-bit the answers differ, from 76 for my own simple conversion to 105 for a GGUF file and up to 182 for one of the ONNX files. Those are different methods, and some keep parts of the model at higher precision. So when someone says 4-bit, ask which method and what the file size is.

title.text:
Demonstration 1: one small
model, four sizes, measured

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_sizes_7.30x3.90.png
objects.alt: Demonstration 1: one small model, four sizes, measured

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Recorded run, SmolLM2-135M, torch, 6 November 2026.
The areas follow the file sizes.
Four bits would give one eighth. The file is 14%, because the scales add about 8 MB.

slides.notes:
This is a recorded run, and you can watch me repeat it. I loaded the small model, counted its weights, and saved the same numbers four times: at 32, 16, 8 and 4 bits. Then I asked the computer for the size of each file. The boxes are drawn so that the area matches the size.

538 megabytes, 269, 135 and 76. Each step halves it, until the last one. Four bits should give one eighth, about 67 megabytes. The extra eight is the scale numbers that every small group of weights carries so it can be turned back into a number.

title.text:
Smaller costs some quality: 8-bit
barely moved, our rough 4-bit did

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_quality_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Smaller costs some quality: 8-bit barely moved, our rough 4-bit did

objects.text: Recorded run: the same model, three test sentences.

runs.text: This is a very small model, and small models lose more when squeezed.
Published 4-bit methods are smarter than my rough one.
Test any shrunk model on your own cases.

slides.notes:
Does shrinking cost anything?

I asked each version for its average miss on three fixed sentences, and for the three likeliest words after the capital city of Uganda is. At 16 bits the results are identical to 32. At 8 bits they barely move. At 4 bits with my rough conversion the average miss rises from 4.57 to 5.09 and the top word jumps to the, with 56 percent.

Three sentences and one run is a tiny test, and published 4-bit methods keep key parts at higher precision. The lesson is to test a shrunk model on your own cases.

title.text:
Rent, host or own: who runs the
model and where your data sits

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_options_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Rent, host or own: who runs the model and where your data sits

objects.text: Hosting or owning needs weights you may run. That means open weights.

slides.notes:
Think of getting to a meeting. Renting is taking a taxi, and you pay for each ride. Hosting is hiring a car with a driver by the day, and you pay whether it is busy or idle. Owning is buying the vehicle, and you pay for fuel, repairs and a driver.

For a model, renting means a vendor runs it and your data goes to the vendor. Hosting means you run an open weights model on a server you rent, in a place you choose. Owning means your own machines. Each step gives more control and needs more skills.

title.text:
Fixed costs beat pay-per-use
only above a certain volume

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t07_breakeven_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Fixed costs beat pay-per-use only above a certain volume

objects.text: Fixed cost divided by the price of one request gives the break-even.

runs.text: Pay per use: UGX 1,000 a request.
Fixed: UGX 3,000,000 a month.
3,000,000 divided by 1,000 is 3,000 requests a month.

slides.notes:
A finance manager knows this one. The figures here are invented, to show the method, because real prices change often and I give none. Suppose a rented service charges UGX 1,000 a request, and a server you host costs UGX 3,000,000 a month whether it is busy or not.

Divide the fixed cost by the price of one request. You get 3,000. Below 3,000 requests a month renting is cheaper. Above it, hosting wins, before you count the skills and the care it needs. Use your own quotes and your own volume.

title.text: NVF would choose a different route for each task

rows.text: No private data; pay only for use
Customer names and orders leave the company
Read staff payroll and leave files
Sensitive data stays where you choose
Search a large private contract archive
Heavy daily use and confidential papers

objects.text: A first view only. Confirm with your lawyer and your IT lead, and test before you commit.

slides.notes:
Here is how Nile Valley Foods might think it through, with an example from each corner of the business. Public product reviews carry no private data, so renting is the simple answer. Customer emails hold names and orders, so rent only after you have read the vendor’s data terms.

Payroll and leave files are the most sensitive, so hosting keeps the data where you choose. A large private contract archive is confidential and used heavily every day, so hosting may also pay. These are first views. Your lawyer and your IT lead should confirm each one.

Now your decision. Which route fits the first model you would use, given your data and your skills?

Rent is the quick start, and you read the data terms. Host gives control and needs a person who can run a server. Own gives the most control and needs machines, power and people. Wait is a real answer too, if your data or your use policy is not ready.

Write your route and the single thing that would change your mind. Is it volume, sensitivity of the data, or a licence limit?

title.text:
Four questions expose a
loose use of the word open

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.75.png

objects.text: Ask the vendor

runs.text: Open source or open weights?
Which licence and limits?
Which container and bits?
Which hardware?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.75.png

objects.text: Listen for

runs.text: A licence you can read
A file size and bit count
A test on your own cases
Who updates and secures it

objects.text: No licence name and no file size means no decision yet.

slides.notes:
Here is the checklist to carry into any vendor meeting. Ask whether the model is open source or open weights. Ask which licence it is under and which uses it limits. Ask which container and how many bits the file uses. Ask which hardware it needs. Then listen.

You want a named licence you can read, a file size and a bit count, a quality test on your own cases, and a clear owner for updates and security. If you hear only the word open, you have no decision yet. Session 13 turns this into the vendor question list.

We began with this question: What does it mean to own, host or rent a model? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
